steps.label: KP06 Nonparametric density estimation | Guided study
01 · Nonparametric estimation lets local data shape a density · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: i.i.d. observations; density is probability per unit length, with total area 1.

What choices remain without a density family?

steps.label: 01 · Nonparametric estimation lets local data shape a density · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Nonparametric estimation still needs sampling assumptions and smoothing choices, and often more data.

steps.label: 01 · Nonparametric estimation lets local data shape a density · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Greater flexibility needs enough data to support local detail.

steps.label: 02 · Density height is probability divided by width · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: sample count N, bin count k_N, width b, and constant height inside a bin.

Does height or area represent probability?

steps.label: 02 · Density height is probability divided by width · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A bin has area  p(x)b=k_N/N; a density height may exceed 1, unlike a probability.

steps.label: 02 · Density height is probability divided by width · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Read histogram probability from area, not height alone.

steps.label: 03 · The same observations look different with different bins · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: N=200, seed 5; all three plots use the same mixture sample.

Which plot loses detail or reveals noise?

steps.label: 03 · The same observations look different with different bins · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: The Freedman–Diaconis rule gives b=2IQRN^-1/3≈1.027, or 8 bins here.

steps.label: 03 · The same observations look different with different bins · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Bin width trades lost detail against sampling noise; a default is not a guarantee.

steps.label: 04 · Consistency needs finer bins and more observations per bin · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: growing sample size N, bin width b_N, and local count k_N.

Can finer bins still contain more observations?

steps.label: 04 · Consistency needs finer bins and more observations per bin · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: For m= N bins, the average count rises from 100 at N=10^4 to 1000 at N=10^6; this is one illustrative sequence.

steps.label: 04 · Consistency needs finer bins and more observations per bin · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Sample size must outpace resolution to support local estimates.

steps.label: 05 · Kernel estimation places a small density at each sample · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: nonnegative unit-integral kernel , bandwidth b>0, and dimension l.

Why must a narrower kernel get taller?

steps.label: 05 · Kernel estimation places a small density at each sample · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: A kernel is centered at each observation; scaling height by b^-l preserves unit integral.

steps.label: 05 · Kernel estimation places a small density at each sample · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A density requires averaging and volume correction, not merely stacking curves.

steps.label: 06 · Both very small and very large bandwidths distort shape · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: the same N=80 sample; Gaussian bandwidths 0.05,0.256,1.2.

Which bandwidth smooths away the two peaks?

steps.label: 06 · Both very small and very large bandwidths distort shape · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Small bandwidth follows individual observations; large bandwidth reduces variance but may merge distinct peaks.

steps.label: 06 · Both very small and very large bandwidths distort shape · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Smoothing scale is usually more influential than kernel shape.

steps.label: 07 · More data can support a smaller bandwidth · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: RMS error against the known simulated density; sample sizes 80 and 320.

Where does more data move the error minimum?

steps.label: 07 · More data can support a smaller bandwidth · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: The selected bandwidths are about 0.256,0.173; real applications need a validation criterion without known truth.

steps.label: 07 · More data can support a smaller bandwidth · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: An example’s best bandwidth is not a universal constant.

steps.label: 08 · Add five kernel contributions, then divide by five · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
